newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope condemns abortion, recalls Jewish suffering.
newsitem.headline: Pope condemns abortion, recalls Jewish suffering.

text.p: Pope John Paul strongly condemned abortion on Wednesday and, in a renewed gesture of reconciliation, paid homage to the place of Jews in Poland's heritage.

He also spoke to the largest crowd of his pilgrimage to his homeland when more than 500,000 worshippers, including former President Lech Walesa, thronged the grounds in Czestochowa of the Jasna Gora Monastery, Poland's holiest shrine.

He briefly met Walesa, who with Church support led the Solidarity free trade union's struggle against communism in the 1980s, in a chapel dedicated to the Black Madonna icon of the Virgin Mary whom many Catholic Poles regard as their queen.

Attacking abortion in Kalisz earlier in the day, the 77-year-old Pope said the practice was barbaric and urged Catholics to join the struggle between "the civilisation of life and the civilisation of death."

His tough language, ahead of Poland's parliamentary elections due around September, was music to the ears of pro-Catholic conservative parties seeking to overturn the present social democratic government led by ex-communists.
"A nation which kills its own children is a nation without a future," he said, repeating a phrase he first uttered when Poland's abortion law was liberalised last October.
"A civilisation which rejects the defenceless would deserve to be called a barbarian civilisation even if had great successes in the fields of economics, technology, art and sciences."
Acknowledging the political sensitivity of his words, the Pope departed from his prepared text to add: "It was not easy for me to say this, because I think about my nation, about its future."
The Roman Catholic Church teaches that life begins at the moment of conception and ends with natural death.
In the eight years since strongly Catholic Poland became the first Eastern European country to cast off communism, few issues have been more passionately fought than abortion.
Under communism, abortion was available on demand.
A law restricting it was passed in 1993 while Walesa, a fervent Catholic, was president.
Under the 1993 law, abortion was allowed only when pregnancy posed a threat to a woman's life, resulted from incest or rape or the foetus had severe defects.
The current leftist-dominated parliament liberalised abortion again last October in defiance of Catholic opposition.
Poland's constitutional court reopened the issue last week when it effectively declared parts of the October law unconstitutional, obliging parliament to review it within six months.

The election campaign now gathering pace pits a powerful anti-abortion alliance centered around the pro-Catholic Solidarity union against the secular-minded ex-communists for the lead in opinion polls.
The Solidarity Election Action (AWS), an umbrella group of some 30 conservative parties, put its logo on posters with the Pope's picture in the run-up to the Pontiff's visit.

In remarks at the Kalisz mass which were not prepared in advance, the Pope paid tribute to Jews, millions of whom died in Nazi German concentration camps in Poland during World War Two, and lauded their shared heritage with Poles.

John Paul, who has made reconciliation with Jews a goal of his pontificate, said: "A people who lived with us for many generations remained with us after this terrible death of millions of daughters and sons. Jewish cemeteries scattered around Poland testify to this common past."
The cemeteries "join Jews and Poles because, together, we await the day of judgment and resurrection," he added.
More than five million Jews, many of them Poles, died in the camps the Germans built here. The pre-war Jewish population has shrunk from 3.5 million to 3,500 practising Jews today.
The Pope was later due to travel from Czestochowa to the southern mountain resort of Zakopane where he will have a rest day on Thursday, mid-way through his 11-day visit.
